The must-sees

  • Augustus Bridge

    Bridge · 1910

    A bridge has stood here since the Middle Ages, and Augustus the Strong had it rebuilt in the 1720s. The present bridge was finished in 1910 and took his name again in 1990.

  • Blue Wonder Bridge

    Bridge · 1893

    It opened in 1893 as an engineering feat. At the end of the war in 1945, the story goes, two local men cut the cables that would have blown it up.

    Look for: On the Loschwitz side, two old railways climb the hillside: a funicular and a suspension railway that hangs from its track, opened in 1901.

  • Brühl’s Terrace

    Viewpoint

    Count Heinrich von Brühl turned the old fortifications into a private garden in the 18th century. It later opened to the public and became known as the Balcony of Europe.

    Look for: At the top of the broad stairs from the Schlossplatz, four bronze groups show Morning, Noon, Evening and Night.

  • Church of Our Lady

    Church · 1743

    George Bähr’s Baroque church collapsed two days after the bombing of February 1945 and lay in ruins for decades. It was rebuilt with donations from around the world and consecrated again in 2005.

    Look for: Inside, find the bent, blackened cross that once crowned the old dome. It was pulled from the rubble.

  • Dresden Castle

    Museum

    For centuries the electors and kings of Saxony lived here. Rebuilt after the war, it now holds museums including the treasure chambers of the Green Vault.

    Look for: In the Green Vault, find a single cherry stone carved with about 185 tiny faces.

  • Dresden Cathedral

    Church · 1751

    Gaetano Chiaveri designed it for the Catholic court in a Protestant city, and it was consecrated in 1751. Members of the Wettin dynasty are buried in its crypt.

    Look for: A covered bridge links the church to the palace, so the royal family could reach Mass without going outside.

  • Golden Rider

    Landmark · 1736

    Unveiled in 1736, it shows the Saxon elector who was also King of Poland, dressed as a Roman emperor. The figure is covered in gold leaf.

  • Outer Neustadt

    Neighbourhood

    The quarter escaped the worst of the 1945 bombing. After 1990 it became the city’s alternative and nightlife district.

    Look for: In the Kunsthofpassage courtyards, one blue facade is hung with funnels and pipes that play music when it rains.

  • Procession of Princes

    Landmark · 1907

    First painted in the 1870s, it was transferred to Meissen porcelain tiles in the early 1900s. The tiles survived the 1945 bombing almost undamaged.

    Look for: Walk to the end of the procession: among the scholars and craftsmen is the artist Wilhelm Walther himself.

  • Semper Opera House

    Culture · 1878

    Gottfried Semper designed the second building after his first burned down, and it opened in 1878. Destroyed in 1945, it reopened in 1985, forty years to the day after the bombing.

    Look for: In the middle of the Theaterplatz, King John of Saxony sits on horseback.

  • Zwinger

    Palace

    Augustus the Strong had it built in the early 18th century by architect Matthäus Daniel Pöppelmann and sculptor Balthasar Permoser. Its Old Masters gallery holds Raphael’s Sistine Madonna.

    Look for: In the Sistine Madonna, look at the bottom edge for the two small winged cherubs leaning on the sill, chins in their hands.

How it works

  1. Open Wizzy in Dresden and tap Start walk, or pick a ready-made walk.
  2. Put your phone in your pocket. Wizzy runs in the background, even with the screen locked.
  3. When you pass a place, you get a ping. Open it for the story, or keep walking.

Every place you see gets stamped in your Dresden passport. Your location stays on your phone. No ads, no tracking.
